div.p: Hard real-time systems require predictable performance despite the occurrence of failures. In this paper, we propose a new fault-tolerant priority assignment algorithm based on worst-case response time schedulability analysis for fault-tolerant hard real-time system. This algorithm can be used, together with the schedulability analysis, to effectively improve system fault resilience when the two traditional faulttolerant priority assignment policies cannot improve system fault resilience. Also, we present a faulttolerant priority configuration search algorithm for the proposed for the proposed analysis.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Predictability and fault tolerance are major requirements for complex real-time systems, which are either safety or mission critical. By predictability we mean, whether the system can be proved to capable of meeting its timing constraints, using well-known worst-case response time estimates. A system is faulttolerant if it produces correct results even in the presence of faults [1]. Due to the critical nature of tasks supported by many real-time systems, it is essential that tasks complete before their deadlines even in the presence of processor failures. This makes faulttolerance an inherent requirement of hard real-time systems, so the effects of possible faults have to be taken into account for schedulability analysis for realtime systems [2].

In general, schedulability analysis is mainly based on the relation of the task's worst-case response time and its deadline. When worst-case response time is earlier than the deadline, the system is schedulable, otherwise, the system is unschedulable. How to deal with the relation of them is one of the hottest aspects for fault-tolerant real-time systems.

Response time analysis has recently been extended to cope with the possibility of errors in the system's computation [3]. Modeling the recovery of tasks as alternative tasks which should be executed to recover the system from an erroneous state, the authors have shown that fault tolerance based on error-recovery techniques can be easily modeled by response time analysis. The Real-Time Group of the University of York has always been taking up the schedulability analysis for fault-tolerant real-time systems [3][4][5][6][7]. In [3][4][5], they use the same fixed-priority assignment algorithms as those used under the fault-free assumption. This approach does not consider appropriate priority assignment schemes to calculate priorities of alternative tasks. Moreover, a new faulttolerant priority assignment policy is proposed in [6,7]. This policy considers the recovery of tasks running with higher priorities. This characteristic is very useful since faulty tasks certainly have a shorter period to meet their deadlines. However, the fault-tolerant priority assignment policy, which allows the alternative tasks run at higher priorities, cannot improve system fault resilience in some certain case. In this paper, we propose a new flexible fault-tolerant priority assignment policy that can improve system fault resilience in this case. Our approach is to consider the recovery of higher priority tasks running with lower priorities. Also, we show that the priority assignment policy is very effective in the sense that the fault resilience is maximized as for the proposed analysis. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is evaluated by simulation.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: The next section presents the assumed computation model. Then, the problems of the two former faulttolerant priority assignment policies on the fault resilience are discussed in detail in Section 3. In other words, in this section, we give the main motivation by presenting an illustrative example. Section 4 presents our approach to carrying out the schedulability analysis based on the worst-case response time analysis. In section 5, the method to finding out the optimal faulttolerant priority configuration is given. At last, Section 6 presents our final comments.

div.head: Computation model
div.p: We assume that there is a set = { 1 , 2 ,…, n } of n tasks, called primary tasks that must be scheduled by the system in the absence of faults. Any primary task i in has a period T i , a deadline D i and a worst-case computation time C i . Tasks can be periodic or sporadic. For sporadic tasks the period refers to the minimum inter-arrival time. Each primary task i can have a certain number of alternative tasks associated with it. Each alternative task only corresponds to a given action taken to recover i from a given fault. Any alternative task has a worst-case computation time. For simplicity we denoted i τ as the alternative task whose worst-case computation time i C is the largest one among these worst-case computation time of all alternative tasks associated with i . And we assume that any alternative tasks corresponding to a primary task runs at the same priority level. Thus we only need to refer to i τ as the worst-case alternative task in case of faults in task i . Obviously, i τ has the same deadline as i . So the total response time of i is the sum of the response time of i and that of i τ . Primary tasks are scheduled according to some fixed priority assignment algorithm (e.g. rate monotonic scheduling algorithm [8] or deadline monotonic scheduling algorithm [9]), which attributes a distinct priority to each primary task. We consider n different priority level (1, 2,…, n), where 1 and n represent the highest and the lowest priority level respectively. We denote p i and i p as the priority of i and i τ , respectively. When a primary task, say i , and an alternative task, say j τ , are ready to execute at the same priority level, we assume that j τ is scheduled first.

We consider only the occurrence of temporary software faults in a uniprocessor system where recovery techniques such as recovery blocks, exception handling or task re-execution are appropriate. When a fault hits i during its execution, the system must schedule the alternative task i τ . We also assume that there is no cost associated with any scheduling of primary or altenative tasks. Also, we assume that all faults are detected by the system and there is no fault propagation, which means that faults affect only the executing task.

We assume in the analysis that there is a minimum time between two consecutive error occurrences, T E . The smaller the value of T E is for which we still meet all deadlines, the stronger the system fault resilience is. Thus, we attribute T E to a standard of the ability to tolerate faults.

The traditional response time of task i is the time needed to execute i and all tasks with each of whose priority is higher than p i . We denote I i as the time needed to execute all task j such that p j > p i . Since the fault-tolerant priority levels of tasks may be not equal to their original priority levels, we take the same approach as the fault-tolerant priority improvement policy. The worst-case response time of task i is split into two branches: considering that errors interrupt the execution of any task but i and considering that i may be interrupted by some error. We denote the worst-case response time of internal errors and external as . When some errors occur in the execution of any task but i , the calculation of i 's worst-case response time is based on the priority level of i . For the preemptive time, I i (by ( 1)), any task whose priority is higher than i 's priority interrupts the execution of i . div.head: The Optimal Priority Configuration Search Algorithm
div.p: Up to now we have presented the schedulability analysis for the proposed approach, but have not considered the best priority configuration so that the fault resilience of the task set is minimized. In this section, such an optimal priority configuration search algorithm is proposed according to properties of the former worst-case response time analysis.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: The main contribution of this paper is described as follows. First, we present the shortcoming of the two traditional fault-tolerant priority assignment policies for the system fault resilience. The traditional priority assignment policies include the fault-tolerant priority inheritance approach and the fault-tolerant priority improvement approach. Second, we propose a new priority assignment algorithm, which can be used, together with the presented schedulability analysis, to improve system fault resilience when the two former approaches cannot do it. The proposed schedulability analysis takes into account the fact that the recoveries of tasks may be executed at lower priority levels. The proposed priority assignment algorithm, which uses some properties of the analysis, is very efficient. This is presented by our illustration example.
